exam.title: Mathematics I - Intermediate Exam
exam.subtitle: Advanced Linear and Abstract Algebra
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks. Show complete solution approach for all calculations. Permitted aids: calculator without programming function. Good luck!

exercises.title: Cube roots
exercises.description:
a) Determine all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with $z^3 = -8$.
b) Sketch the solutions in the Gaussian plane (a description suffices) and factor $z^3 + 8$ into real factors.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Polar form
$-8 = 8e^{i\pi}$, so $z_k = \sqrt[3]{8}\,e^{i(\pi + 2\pi k)/3} = 2e^{i\pi(2k+1)/3}$, $k = 0,1,2$.

Step 2: Part a): The three solutions
$z_0 = 2e^{i\pi/3} = 1 + \sqrt3i$, $z_1 = 2e^{i\pi} = -2$, $z_2 = 2e^{5i\pi/3} = 1 - \sqrt3i$. Check: $(1 + \sqrt3i)^3 = 8e^{i\pi} = -8$ ✓ and $(-2)^3 = -8$ ✓.

Step 3: Part b): Geometry
The solutions lie on the circle of radius $2$ at angular spacing $120^\circ$ and form an equilateral triangle. Their sum is $0$.

Step 4: Part b): Real factorisation
$z^3 + 8 = (z + 2)(z - z_0)(z - z_2)$ with $(z - z_0)(z - z_2) = z^2 - 2z + 4$ (sum $z_0 + z_2 = 2$, product $|z_0|^2 = 4$). So $z^3 + 8 = (z+2)(z^2 - 2z + 4)$ — this is the sum formula $a^3 + b^3$ ✓.

exercises.title: Kernel, image and rank–nullity theorem
exercises.description:
Let $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, $f(\vec x) = A\vec x$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Determine $\ker f$.
b) Determine a basis of $\operatorname{im} f$.
c) Verify the rank–nullity theorem.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Row reduction
$R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Row swap: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, rank $2$.

Step 2: Part a): Kernel
From the second row $z = 0$, from the first $x = -2y$ with free $y$. $\ker f = \operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,0)\}$. Check: $A(-2,1,0)^T = (-2 + 2,\ -4 + 4,\ -2 + 2) = \vec0$ ✓.

Step 3: Part b): Image
The pivot columns (columns 1 and 3) of the **original** matrix form a basis of the column space: $\operatorname{im} f = \operatorname{span}\{(1,2,1),(1,2,0)\}$. (Column 2 $= 2\cdot$ column 1.)

Step 4: Part c): Rank–nullity theorem
$\dim\ker f + \dim\operatorname{im} f = 1 + 2 = 3 = \dim\mathbb{R}^3$ ✓. Consequence: $f$ is neither injective nor surjective; the image is the plane $y = 2x$ ✓.

exercises.title: Euclidean algorithm for polynomials
exercises.description:
a) Determine $\gcd(x^3 - 1,\ x^2 - 1)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
b) Give a generator of the ideal $(x^3 - 1,\ x^2 - 1)$.
c) Show that $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^2 - 2)$ is a field.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Division with remainder
$x^3 - 1 = x\,(x^2 - 1) + (x - 1)$. Then $x^2 - 1 = (x+1)(x - 1) + 0$. The last non-zero remainder is $x - 1$: $\gcd = x - 1$.

Step 2: Part b): Ideal
$\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is a principal ideal domain: $(x^3-1,\ x^2-1) = (\gcd) = (x - 1)$. Check: $x - 1 = (x^3 - 1) - x(x^2 - 1)$ lies in the ideal, and conversely both generators are multiples of $x - 1$ ✓.

Step 3: Part c): Irreducibility
$x^2 - 2$ has no root in $\mathbb{Q}$ since $\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$; a degree-$2$ polynomial without root is irreducible.

Step 4: Part c): Field
In a principal ideal domain the ideal generated by an irreducible element is maximal, hence $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^2-2)$ is a field. It is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ with elements $a + b\bar x$, $\bar x^2 = 2$.

exercises.title: Diagonalisation and matrix power
exercises.description:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Determine eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
b) Find a formula for $A^n$ and check it for $n = 1,2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Eigenvalues
$\operatorname{tr}A = 7$, $\det A = 10$: $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = 0$, so $\lambda_1 = 5$, $\lambda_2 = 2$.

Step 2: Part a): Eigenvectors
$\lambda = 5$: $A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $(1,1)^T$. $\lambda = 2$: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $(2,-1)^T$.

Step 3: Part b): Diagonalisation
$S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $S^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(5,2)$. Then $A^n = SD^nS^{-1} = 5^nP_5 + 2^nP_2$ with the projectors $P_5 = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $P_2 = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Part b): Formula
$A^n = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 5^n + 2^{n+1} & 2\cdot5^n - 2^{n+1} \\ 5^n - 2^n & 2\cdot5^n + 2^n \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Part b): Checks
$n = 1$: $\frac13\begin{pmatrix} 5+4 & 10-4 \\ 5-2 & 10+2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = A$ ✓. $n = 2$: $\frac13\begin{pmatrix} 25+8 & 50-8 \\ 25-4 & 50+4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 & 14 \\ 7 & 18 \end{pmatrix} = A^2$ ✓ (directly: $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}^2$).

exercises.title: Computing in 𝔽₇ and 𝔽₉
exercises.description:
a) Determine in $\mathbb{F}_7$ the inverse of $3$ and solve $3x + 2 = 5$.
b) Which elements of $\mathbb{F}_7$ are squares? Solve $x^2 = 2$ and $x^2 = 3$.
c) Show that $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_3$ and compute in $\mathbb{F}_9 = \mathbb{F}_3[x]/(x^2+1)$ the product $(1+x)(1-x)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Inverse and linear equation
$3\cdot5 = 15 \equiv 1$, so $3^{-1} = 5$. $3x + 2 = 5 \iff 3x = 3 \iff x = 5\cdot3 = 15 \equiv 1$. Check: $3 + 2 = 5$ ✓.

Step 2: Part b): Squares in 𝔽₇
$1^2 = 1$, $2^2 = 4$, $3^2 = 9 \equiv 2$, $4^2 = 16 \equiv 2$, $5^2 = 25 \equiv 4$, $6^2 = 36 \equiv 1$. Squares: $\{0,1,2,4\}$. $x^2 = 2$ has the solutions $x = 3$ and $x = 4$ ($= -3$). $x^2 = 3$ has **no** solution ($3$ is not a square).

Step 3: Part c): Irreducibility over 𝔽₃
$0^2 + 1 = 1$, $1^2 + 1 = 2$, $2^2 + 1 = 5 \equiv 2$: no root. A degree-$2$ polynomial without root is irreducible, so $\mathbb{F}_3[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field with $3^2 = 9$ elements.

Step 4: Part c): Product
$(1+x)(1-x) = 1 - x^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$ (because $x^2 = -1$). Check by expanding: $1 - x + x - x^2 = 1 - x^2$ ✓.

exercises.title: Gram-Schmidt and orthogonal projection
exercises.description:
Let $U = \operatorname{span}\{\vec v_1,\vec v_2\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ with $\vec v_1 = (1,1,0)$, $\vec v_2 = (1,0,1)$.
a) Determine an orthonormal basis of $U$ with the Gram-Schmidt process.
b) Determine the orthogonal projection of $\vec b = (1,2,3)$ onto $U$ and verify that the remainder is perpendicular to $U$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): First vector
$\vec u_1 = \frac{\vec v_1}{|\vec v_1|} = \frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,0)$.

Step 2: Part a): Second vector
Orthogonalise: $\vec w_2 = \vec v_2 - (\vec v_2\cdot\vec u_1)\vec u_1 = (1,0,1) - \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0) = \left(\frac12,-\frac12,1\right)$. Norm: $|\vec w_2| = \sqrt{\frac14 + \frac14 + 1} = \sqrt{\frac32}$. $\vec u_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2)$.

Step 3: Part b): Projection
$P\vec b = (\vec b\cdot\vec u_1)\vec u_1 + (\vec b\cdot\vec u_2)\vec u_2$. $\vec b\cdot\vec u_1 = \frac{3}{\sqrt2}$, $\vec b\cdot\vec u_2 = \frac{1 - 2 + 6}{\sqrt6} = \frac{5}{\sqrt6}$. $P\vec b = \frac32(1,1,0) + \frac56(1,-1,2) = \left(\frac73,\frac23,\frac53\right)$.

Step 4: Part b): Orthogonality check
Remainder: $\vec b - P\vec b = \left(-\frac43,\frac43,\frac43\right)$. $\cdot\vec v_1 = -\frac43 + \frac43 = 0$ ✓ and $\cdot\vec v_2 = -\frac43 + \frac43 = 0$ ✓. The remainder is perpendicular to $U$; $|\vec b - P\vec b| = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}$ is the distance from $\vec b$ to the plane $U$.
